lessons.title: The East India Company and Its Trade
lessons.notes_html:
Foundation of the Company

The East India Company was established by the British traders (merchants) of England in 1600 CE, after getting royal permission (a charter) from the Queen of England, for the purpose of trade with India and the East.

Arrival in India

The Company's ships first came to the port of Surat on 24 August 1608 CE. In 1612 CE it defeated the Portuguese in India and won trading concessions from the Mughal Empire, and in 1613 CE a Farman (royal order) was issued by the Mughal emperor Jahangir allowing the Company to establish a factory in Surat.

What the Company Traded

The Company traded mainly in spices, silk, cotton (cotton and silk goods/cloth), indigo, dye, tea and saltpeter. It bought these Indian goods cheaply and sold them in Europe at huge profits. Indian goods were in great demand in Europe, and Arab and Portuguese traders were already earning huge profits, so the British also wished to trade with India.

From Trade to Rule

Although the Company was established for trade, it gradually became involved in the politics of the subcontinent. By winning the Battles of Plassey (1757 CE) and Buxar (1764 CE) it became the real ruler of Bengal and then of most of India, until after the War of Independence 1857 CE the British Crown took over India directly in 1858 CE.

lessons.title: The Battles of Plassey and Buxar
lessons.notes_html:
The Battle of Plassey 1757 CE

The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 CE. It was won by the British East India Company under Robert Clive against Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah of Bengal. The British won mainly through treachery: Clive had secretly won over Mir Jaffar, the commander-in-chief (Mir Bakhshi) of the Nawab's army, by promising him the throne of Bengal. During the battle Mir Jaffar kept the largest part of the Nawab's army standing idle, so the Nawab's small loyal force was defeated; Siraj-ud-Daulah fled and was later killed. Mir Jaffar was made the new Nawab, but he remained a puppet in British hands — his betrayal laid the foundation of British rule in India.

Causes of the Battle of Buxar

After Plassey, the British replaced Mir Jaffar with Mir Qasim, who tried to free himself from British control: he reformed his army and administration and removed duties that gave the British an unfair trade advantage. The British declared war on him. Mir Qasim joined hands with Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh) and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

Result of Buxar 1764 CE

In the Battle of Buxar (1764 CE) the British under Major Munro defeated the combined armies of the three rulers. By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765 CE) the Company obtained the Diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from the Mughal emperor. The victory of Buxar confirmed and completed what Plassey had begun — the British became the real masters of eastern India.

lessons.title: Mysore: Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan
lessons.notes_html:
Haider Ali of Mysore

Haider Ali was the ruler of the state of Mysore in South India. He and his son Tipu Sultan were the strongest Indian opponents of the British in the south, and the British fought a series of Anglo-Mysore wars against them. Tipu Sultan died fighting the British in 1799 CE in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War at Seringapatam.

Why the British Defeated Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan

The solved Learning Activities give the reasons: the British had a better organised and disciplined army, modern weapons, strong sea power and greater financial resources. They also used diplomacy to divide the Indian rulers — the Marathas and the Nizam joined the British against Mysore — and the Indian states were not united, so the British defeated them one by one.

Timeline of the Company's Rise

  • 1600 CE — East India Company established
  • 1608 CE — Company reaches Surat
  • 1757 CE — Battle of Plassey
  • 1764 CE — Battle of Buxar
  • 1799 CE — Death of Tipu Sultan (Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Seringapatam)
  • 1857 CE — War of Independence

lessons.title: The Doctrine of Lapse
lessons.notes_html:
The Policy

The Doctrine of Lapse was a policy introduced by Lord Dalhousie (Governor General) in 1852 CE (applied from 1848 CE). Under it, if an Indian ruler of a state under British protection died without a natural male heir, his state would not pass to an adopted son but would 'lapse' — that is, be annexed by the British.

States Annexed

By this policy several states were annexed, most famously Jhansi (the state of Rani Lakshmi Bai's husband), Satara and Nagpur.

Effects of the Policy

Indian rulers and people became angry and fearful, because adoption was an old and sacred custom of the Hindus. The policy destroyed the trust of the Indian princes in the British, created great resentment among Indians, and became one of the major causes of the War of Independence 1857 CE, in which the Rani of Jhansi became a leading heroine.

lessons.title: The War of Independence 1857 CE
lessons.notes_html:
Political Causes

The British annexed Indian states one after another; Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse annexed states like Jhansi, and the Mughal emperor was insulted and threatened with the loss of his title.

Economic, Social and Military Causes

Economic: Indian industries and trade were destroyed by British policies, heavy taxes ruined farmers, and Indian goods could not compete with British machine-made goods. Social/religious: the British interfered in the religion and customs of the people; Christian missionaries were active, and Indians feared forcible conversion. Military: Indian soldiers were paid less and treated as inferior to British soldiers, and were sent across the sea against their beliefs.

The Immediate Cause

The immediate cause was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle cartridges, which the soldiers had to bite before loading. It was rumoured (and believed) that the cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs — the cow being sacred to Hindus and the pig forbidden (haram) for Muslims. This hurt the religious feelings of both Hindu and Muslim soldiers; the revolt of the soldiers at Meerut sparked the War of Independence.

The Black Hole Incident and the Aftermath

The Black Hole incident is related to the capture of Calcutta by Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah in 1756 CE: according to the British account, British prisoners were locked in a very small dark room for a night and many died of suffocation; the British used it to provoke anger against the Nawab before Plassey. After the War of 1857 failed, Lord Canning read out the proclamation of Queen Victoria at Allahabad, and the British Crown took India over directly in 1858 CE.

lessons.title: Muslims after the War of Independence 1857
lessons.notes_html:
Religious Condition

After the War of Independence 1857 CE, the condition of the Muslims was miserable in every field. The British blamed the Muslims for the war; mosques and madrassas were closed or destroyed, religious endowments were confiscated, and the Muslims feared Christian missionary pressure.

Political Condition

The Mughal Empire ended and Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon. Muslims were removed from government jobs and their lands and properties were seized; they had no political party or representation.

Educational Condition

The Muslims, distrusting the British, refused to adopt the new English education, while their own madrassa system had decayed. As a result they fell far behind the Hindus in education, jobs and business, and became poor and backward. It was in these conditions that reformers like Sir Syed Ahmed Khan came forward to revive the Muslims.

lessons.title: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan: Life and Reconciliation
lessons.notes_html:
Early Life

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan was born in 1817 CE in Delhi. At the time of the War of Independence 1857 he was at Bijnor, where he saved British families during the revolt. He died at Aligarh in 1898 CE.

Removing British Distrust

After 1857 the British considered the Muslims their enemies and the Muslims hated the British; Sir Syed worked to remove this enmity from both sides. He wrote 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (The Causes of the Indian Revolt, 1858 CE) explaining to the British that the revolt was not only the Muslims' fault but resulted from British policies and the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council. He wrote 'The Loyal Muhammadans of India' to show that many Muslims had remained loyal and had even saved British lives.

Advising the Muslims

He advised the Muslims to give up confrontation, adopt modern education and cooperate with the government for their own progress. In this way he built a bridge of reconciliation between the British rulers and the Muslims.

His Books

Two famous books of Sir Syed are 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind' (1858 CE) and 'Asar-us-Sanadid', about the historical buildings and people of Delhi. His 'Khutbat-e-Ahmadia' and his commentary on the Holy Quran are also famous.

lessons.title: The Aligarh Movement: Educational Services
lessons.notes_html:
Schools and the Scientific Society

Sir Syed's educational services are the heart of the Aligarh Movement. He established a school at Moradabad (1859 CE) and a school at Ghazipur (1864 CE). He founded the Scientific Society at Ghazipur in 1863 CE, which translated English books of science and literature into Urdu.

Journals

He started the Aligarh Institute Gazette in 1866 CE — a bilingual (Urdu-English) journal of the Scientific Society, published to spread modern knowledge and his reform ideas among the Muslims — and the journal 'Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq' (1870 CE) to reform Muslim society.

MAO School and College

He established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) High School at Aligarh in 1875 CE, which became MAO College in 1877 CE — and later, in 1920 CE, Aligarh Muslim University. He also founded the Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886 CE) to spread education among Muslims all over India. Through these services he persuaded the Muslims to acquire modern English education, the key to their revival.

lessons.title: Sir Syed as a Social Reformer and the Two-Nation Theory
lessons.notes_html:
Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq

As a social reformer, Sir Syed tried to remove the backwardness and harmful customs of Muslim society. Through his journal 'Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq' (1870 CE) he attacked ignorance, superstition and useless customs and promoted morality, cleanliness, hard work and rational thinking.

His Reform Message

He urged the Muslims to give up their hatred of English education, to adopt modern sciences, and to improve the condition of women through education. For religious education, he wrote a commentary (Tafsir) of the Holy Quran and books like 'Khutbat-e-Ahmadia' defending Islam against the objections of Christian writers, and he arranged religious instruction along with modern education in his institutions at Aligarh.

The Two-Nation Theory

Sir Syed promoted Hindu-Muslim unity in his early life, calling Hindus and Muslims 'the two eyes of India'. But after the Urdu-Hindi controversy (1867 CE) he concluded that Hindus and Muslims differed in religion, culture, language, law and heroes, and that the Hindu majority, once in power, would dominate the Muslims. Hence they were two separate nations who could not live under one political system — the Two-Nation Theory, which later became the basis of Pakistan.

Timeline of the Movement

  • 1817 — born in Delhi; 1858 — 'Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind'
  • 1859 — school at Moradabad; 1863 — Scientific Society
  • 1866 — Aligarh Institute Gazette; 1870 — 'Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq'
  • 1875 — MAO High School; 1877 — MAO College

Darul Uloom Deoband and Nadva-tul-Ulema

Darul-Uloom-Deoband was founded in 1866 CE. Nadva-tul-Ulema, Lucknow (founded 1894 CE) was founded by Maulana Muhammad Ali Mungeri along with other scholars; it aimed at reforming religious education by combining the old religious sciences with modern knowledge.

Sindh Madrasa and Islamia College

Sindh Madrasa-tul-Islam, Karachi was founded by Hassan Ali Afandi, and Islamia College Peshawar by Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum.

Muhammadan Educational Conference

The Muhammadan Educational Conference was established by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan in 1886 CE. Its objectives were: to promote modern education among the Muslims; to discuss their educational problems and find solutions; to spread the message of the Aligarh movement to every part of India; and to create unity and political awareness among the Muslims. It held annual sessions in different cities, passed resolutions for Muslim education and encouraged the establishment of schools and colleges. It was in its annual session at Dhaka in 1906 that the All India Muslim League was founded.

Significance of Modern Institutions

Modern educational institutions are highly significant for Pakistan: they produce educated citizens, doctors, engineers, teachers and officers; they spread science and technology; they created the leadership that won Pakistan (the students of Aligarh played a leading role in the Pakistan Movement); and they keep our religious and cultural identity alive along with modern knowledge.

lessons.title: World War I: Causes and Outbreak
lessons.notes_html:
Span of the War

World War-I lasted from 1914 CE to 1918 CE (about four years). It started in 1914 and ended in November 1918 with the defeat of Germany and its allies.

Major Causes

  • Rivalry and competition among the European powers for colonies and trade in Asia and Africa
  • The alliance system: Europe was divided into two armed camps — the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) — so a quarrel between two countries could drag in all
  • Militarism: an arms race, especially the naval race between Britain and Germany
  • Imperialism and nationalism: extreme love of one's own nation and hatred of others, e.g. Serbian nationalism in the Balkans

The Immediate Cause

The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, by a Serbian nationalist at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 CE. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and because of the system of alliances the great powers of Europe were drawn into the war one after another.

lessons.title: Events of World War I and the Ottoman Empire
lessons.notes_html:
Main Events of the War

  • 1914 CE — Germany attacked France through Belgium; Britain declared war on Germany; the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers; trench warfare began on the Western Front
  • 1915 CE — Italy joined the Allies; the Gallipoli campaign against the Ottomans failed
  • 1916 CE — the great Battles of Verdun and the Somme caused huge losses
  • 1917 CE — the USA joined the Allies; the Russian Revolution took place and Russia left the war
  • 1918 CE — Germany's final offensives failed; Germany signed the armistice on 11 November 1918
  • 1919 CE — the Treaty of Versailles formally settled the peace with Germany

Role of the Ottoman Empire

The Ottoman Empire joined World War-I on the side of the Central Powers (Germany and Austria-Hungary) in 1914 CE. It closed the Dardanelles strait, cutting Russia's supply route; the Allies attacked Gallipoli (1915) to open it but were defeated by the Turks under Mustafa Kemal. Ottoman forces fought the British in Mesopotamia (Iraq), Palestine and Arabia, where the Arabs, encouraged by Britain, revolted against the Turks (the Arab Revolt).

Break-up of the Ottoman Empire

After its defeat in 1918, the Ottoman Empire was broken up: its Arab territories (Palestine, Syria, Iraq, Arabia) were taken away and divided between Britain and France as mandates, and the Khilafat (Caliphate) itself was abolished by Turkey in 1924 CE — an event which deeply affected the Muslims of India and led to the Khilafat Movement.

lessons.title: World War II: Causes and India's Role
lessons.notes_html:
Outbreak of the War

World War-II started in 1939 CE — on 1 September 1939, when Germany under Adolf Hitler attacked Poland; Britain and France then declared war on Germany. It lasted until 1945 CE.

Causes of World War-II

  • The harsh Treaty of Versailles (1919) humiliated Germany with heavy fines (reparations), loss of territory and limits on its army, creating a desire for revenge
  • The rise of dictators: Hitler in Germany and Mussolini in Italy preached aggressive nationalism and expansion
  • The Great Economic Depression (1929) created unemployment and instability which dictators exploited
  • The failure of the League of Nations to stop aggression (Japan in Manchuria, Italy in Ethiopia)
  • The policy of appeasement by Britain and France, which encouraged Hitler

Role of Indians in World War-II

India was made a part of World War-II by Britain without consulting Indian leaders. More than two million Indian soldiers — the largest volunteer army of the war — fought for the Allies in North Africa, Italy, the Middle East and especially in Burma against Japan, and their role was decisive in stopping the Japanese advance towards India. At the same time, many Indians opposed the war effort: the Congress launched the Quit India Movement (1942), and Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) with Japanese support. The war weakened Britain greatly, and after it ended in 1945 Britain could no longer hold India — independence came in 1947.

lessons.title: The Cold War
lessons.notes_html:
What was the Cold War?

The Cold War was the long period of tension and rivalry (roughly 1945–1991 CE) between the two superpowers that emerged from World War-II — the capitalist USA and the communist Soviet Union (USSR) — and their allies. It is called 'cold' because the two never fought a direct war, fearing nuclear destruction.

How it was Fought

Instead of direct war, the superpowers competed through the arms race, the space race, propaganda, espionage and proxy wars (e.g. Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan). The USA made the pact of NATO — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (1949 CE) — with its European allies; in response, the Soviet Union formed the Warsaw Pact with its allies in 1955 CE.

Why it Began

The wartime allies had opposite ideologies and aims: the USSR set up communist governments in Eastern Europe as a protective belt, while the USA tried to stop the spread of communism (containment). Mutual distrust, the division of Germany and the race for influence over the world divided the globe into two hostile blocs.

lessons.title: The United Nations and the Consequences of World War II
lessons.notes_html:
The United Nations

The United Nations (UN) was established in 1945 CE after World War-II. Its headquarters are in New York, USA, and the International Court of Justice is based in The Hague, Netherlands.

Basic Functions of the UN

  • To maintain international peace and security and prevent wars, settling disputes between countries peacefully
  • To develop friendly relations among nations
  • To promote human rights and fundamental freedoms
  • To achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, health and humanitarian problems through agencies like WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO and FAO
  • To provide help in disasters and to protect refugees

Consequences of World War-II

The war killed about 60 million people, including the victims of the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (Japan), and caused great destruction of cities and economies. Germany was divided into East and West Germany, and Europe into two blocs. The USA and the USSR emerged as two superpowers and the Cold War began. The colonial empires of Britain and France weakened, and many countries of Asia and Africa, including Pakistan and India (1947), gained independence. New deadly weapons, especially nuclear weapons, changed warfare forever.

lessons.notes_html:
The Indian National Congress

The Indian National Congress was established in 1885 CE in the city of Bombay. Gradually it became a Hindu-dominated body which claimed to represent all Indians but ignored Muslim interests.

The Partition of Bengal 1905

The Partition of Bengal (1905 CE) favoured the Muslims: the new province of East Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority with Dhaka as its capital, ending the domination of the Hindu landlords, lawyers and money-lenders of Calcutta. Muslims got more jobs, educational institutions and development in their neglected region, and it awakened them politically. When the partition was annulled in 1911 CE under Hindu pressure, the Muslims learned that they needed their own political party.

The Simla Deputation 1906

The Simla Deputation — a delegation of 35 Muslim leaders which met the Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla on 1 October 1906 — was led by Sir Aga Khan (Aga Khan III). It demanded separate electorates and representation for the Muslims, which the Viceroy promised to accept. Its success encouraged the Muslim leaders to found their own political party.

lessons.title: The Muslim League: Background, Establishment and Objectives
lessons.notes_html:
Background

Several events formed the background of the Muslim League's establishment: after 1857 the Muslims were backward in education and jobs, and Sir Syed's movement awakened them politically; the Congress (founded 1885) gradually became a Hindu-dominated body; the Urdu-Hindi controversy (1867) convinced the Muslims that their rights could not be protected by the Congress; the Partition of Bengal (1905) controversy taught them the need for their own organization; and the success of the Simla Deputation (October 1906) encouraged the leaders.

Establishment

The All India Muslim League was established on 30 December 1906 CE at Dhaka, during the annual session of the Muhammadan Educational Conference. Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dhaka proposed its formation; Aga Khan was elected its first President.

Objectives

  • To protect and advance the political rights and interests of the Muslims of India and represent their needs to the government
  • To promote among the Muslims feelings of loyalty to the British government and remove misunderstandings
  • To promote feelings of friendliness between the Muslims and other communities of India

Under Quaid-e-Azam's leadership its objective later developed into the demand for a separate homeland — Pakistan, achieved in 1947.

lessons.title: The Lucknow Pact and the Khilafat Movement
lessons.notes_html:
The Lucknow Pact 1916

The Lucknow Pact (1916 CE) was an agreement between the Muslim League and the Congress, largely due to the efforts of Quaid-e-Azam, then called the 'Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity'. Its important points: both parties jointly demanded self-government (Home Rule) for India; the Congress accepted the Muslim demand of separate electorates; Muslims would get one-third of the elected seats in the Central Legislature and fixed shares in the provinces (e.g. 50% in Punjab, 40% in Bengal); and no law concerning a community would be passed if three-fourths of that community's members opposed it.

The Khilafat Movement 1919-1924

The Khilafat Movement (1919-1924 CE) was launched by the Muslims of India to protect the Ottoman Caliphate (Khilafat) and the holy places of Islam after the defeat of Turkey in World War-I. The British had promised not to harm the Khilafat, but after the war they divided the Ottoman Empire. Under the leadership of the Ali Brothers (Maulana Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Maulana Shaukat Ali), Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and others, the Muslims protested, boycotted British goods and cooperated with Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement; thousands migrated towards Afghanistan in the Hijrat Movement.

End and Importance

The Moplah rising and the Chauri Chaura incident (1922) led Gandhi to end Non-Cooperation, and in 1924 Mustafa Kemal Ataturk himself abolished the Khilafat in Turkey, ending the movement. Its importance: it politically awakened the Muslims of India, trained them in mass struggle and brought ulema and western-educated Muslims together — experience which later served the Pakistan Movement.

lessons.title: Nehru Report, Fourteen Points and Civil Disobedience
lessons.notes_html:
The Nehru Report 1928

The Nehru Report (1928 CE) was a constitutional proposal prepared by a committee under Motilal Nehru. The Muslims refused to accept it because it rejected separate electorates, gave them no proper share (one-third) in the central legislature, opposed residuary powers for the provinces, and proposed a unitary (strong-centre) system. Quaid-e-Azam called it a 'parting of the ways' and replied with his Fourteen Points.

The Fourteen Points 1929

Quaid-e-Azam presented his Fourteen Points in 1929 CE. Their highlights: a federal system with residuary powers with the provinces; uniform provincial autonomy; adequate minority representation; one-third Muslim representation in the Central Legislature; continuation of separate electorates; no territorial change affecting the Muslim majority in Punjab, Bengal and NWFP; full religious freedom; Sindh separated from Bombay; reforms in NWFP and Balochistan; adequate Muslim share in the services; protection of Muslim culture, education, language and personal law; one-third Muslim ministers in cabinets; and no constitutional change without the consent of the federating units. These points became the basic charter of Muslim demands.

The Civil Disobedience Movement 1930

The Civil Disobedience Movement was started by Gandhi and the Congress in 1930 CE to protest against British rule and press for complete independence (Purna Swaraj). It began with Gandhi's Salt March to Dandi, where he broke the salt law; people refused to obey British laws, boycotted foreign goods and did not pay taxes. The Muslim League kept aloof, because the Muslims had lost trust in the Congress after the Nehru Report, so Hindu-Muslim unity weakened and the two nations moved towards the demand for separate homelands.

The Round Table Conferences

The First Round Table Conference was held in 1930 CE in London to discuss India's constitutional future. Further conferences followed in 1931 and 1932; the Civil Disobedience Movement was interrupted by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) so that the Congress could attend.

The Communal Award 1932

The Communal Award was presented in 1932 CE by the British government, announcing separate electorates and seat shares for the different communities. Coming after the failure of the conferences to agree, it further widened the gulf between Hindus and Muslims.

The Cripps Proposals 1942

The Cripps Proposals were presented in 1942 CE, during World War-II, offering India dominion status after the war. Both the Congress and the Muslim League rejected them. After their failure, the Congress launched the Quit India Movement in August 1942 CE to compel the British to leave India immediately and hand over power to the Indians. The Muslim League did not join it, considering it a move to establish Congress (Hindu) rule.

lessons.title: The Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution 1940
lessons.notes_html:
The Lahore Session

The annual session of the All India Muslim League was held at Minto Park, Lahore (22-24 March 1940 CE), presided over by Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The Lahore Resolution was presented by A. K. Fazlul Haq (the Tiger of Bengal) and passed on 23 March 1940 CE.

The Demand

The Resolution demanded that the Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones of India should be grouped to constitute 'Independent States' in which the constituent units would be autonomous and sovereign — in other words, a separate homeland for the Muslims.

Why it is Called the Pakistan Resolution

The Hindu press and newspapers immediately nicknamed it the 'Pakistan Resolution' — because the state it demanded was the Pakistan proposed by Chaudhry Rahmat Ali (1933). The name became so popular that the Resolution is remembered by it; and when Pakistan was created on 14 August 1947, the demand of the Lahore Resolution was fulfilled.

Deliverance Day and the Lyallpur Address

When the Congress ministries resigned in 1939, Quaid-e-Azam advised the Muslims to celebrate a Deliverance Day in 1939 CE. At a meeting at Dhobi Ghat, Lyallpur (Faisalabad) in 1942 CE, he assured the minorities: 'Pakistan would be the solution of all problems of minorities', and equal rights would be granted to all minorities in Pakistan. His leadership — uniting the Muslims, arguing their case constitutionally and winning a homeland within seven years of the Resolution — rightly earned him the title Quaid-e-Azam (the Great Leader).

lessons.title: Early Problems of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Administrative and Refugee Problems

Pakistan faced many severe problems after independence in 1947 CE. Administrative: there was no capital, no offices, no trained staff; government had to be set up from nothing, with Quaid-e-Azam as the first Governor General and Liaquat Ali Khan as Prime Minister. Refugee: about 7 million Muslim refugees poured in from India, homeless and penniless, and had to be fed, sheltered and resettled, while communal massacres took a heavy toll.

Division of Assets

Pakistan's share in the division of assets was 17.5 percent. In the cash balances, Pakistan's share came to Rs. 750 million; India paid only Rs. 200 million at first and released the remaining Rs. 550 million later (in January 1948, after Gandhi's fast). Pakistan also received its 17.5% share of the military stores and other government assets, though much of it was delivered late or in damaged condition.

Other Problems

Canal water dispute: India cut off the water of the canals flowing into Pakistan (1948), threatening its agriculture. Accession of princely states: disputes over Junagadh, Hyderabad and above all Kashmir, which led to the first Kashmir war (1947-48) and remains unsolved. Financial: almost no industry, banks or treasury. Constitutional: no constitution; the state ran on the amended Government of India Act 1935, and framing a constitution took nine years. In spite of all these problems, Pakistan survived and consolidated itself by the determination of its leaders and people.

lessons.title: The Objectives Resolution 1949
lessons.notes_html:
Passing of the Resolution

The Objectives Resolution was passed in 1949 CE by the Constituent Assembly, presented by Liaquat Ali Khan. It is one of the most important documents in the constitutional history of Pakistan.

Salient Features

  • Sovereignty over the entire universe belongs to Allah Almighty alone, and the authority exercised by the people of Pakistan is a sacred trust within the limits prescribed by Him
  • The state shall exercise its powers through the chosen representatives of the people
  • The principles of democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance and social justice, as enunciated by Islam, shall be fully observed
  • Muslims shall be enabled to order their lives in accordance with the Holy Quran and Sunnah
  • Adequate provision shall be made for the minorities to freely profess and practise their religions and develop their cultures
  • The judiciary shall be independent, and fundamental rights of all citizens shall be guaranteed

Importance

The Resolution laid down the basic principles on which the future constitution of Pakistan would be framed. It became the preamble of the constitutions of 1956, 1962 and 1973, and in 1985 it was made a substantive part of the 1973 Constitution as Article 2-A. It defines Pakistan as an Islamic democratic state.

lessons.title: Constitutions of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
The First Constitution 1956

Pakistan adopted its first Constitution in 1956 CE. It was enforced on 23 March 1956, and Pakistan became the 'Islamic Republic of Pakistan'. (It was abrogated in 1958 when Ayub Khan imposed martial law; his own Constitution followed in 1962.)

The 1973 Constitution

  • It is a written and detailed constitution, framed by the elected National Assembly and passed unanimously
  • Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic — the Prime Minister is the chief executive, the President the head of state
  • Islam is the state religion; the Objectives Resolution is its preamble (later Article 2-A), and no law can be made against the Quran and Sunnah
  • It guarantees fundamental rights to all citizens — freedom, equality before law, and protection of minorities
  • It provides an independent judiciary with a Supreme Court and High Courts
  • The legislature (Majlis-e-Shoora) has two houses: the National Assembly and the Senate
  • Urdu is the national language
  • It is a rigid constitution — amendable only by a two-thirds majority of the Parliament

The 1973 Constitution was enforced on 14 August 1973 and, with amendments, is the constitution of Pakistan today.

lessons.title: Wars, Treaties and Foreign Relations
lessons.notes_html:
The 3rd June Plan and UN Membership

The 3rd June Plan was presented in 1947 CE, announcing the partition of India. Pakistan became a member of the United Nations in 1947 CE (30 September 1947). The United Nations sent a representative to India and Pakistan to review the Kashmir issue in 1951 CE.

The Indus Waters Treaty 1960

Under the Indus Waters (Indus Basin) Treaty of 1960 CE, Pakistan conceded the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India, while the waters of the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — were allocated to Pakistan (India being allowed only limited use of them).

The Indo-Pak War 1965

Causes: the unresolved Kashmir dispute was the basic cause; the Rann of Kutch clash (April 1965) raised tensions; and in August 1965 fighting started in Kashmir, after which India attacked across the international border. Events: on 6 September 1965 India attacked Lahore and other fronts without a formal declaration of war; Pakistan's armed forces and people defended the country bravely — Major Aziz Bhatti (Nishan-e-Haider) fell defending Lahore; the Pakistan Air Force struck heavy blows, with M. M. Alam's famous record of shooting down five Indian planes in a minute; fierce tank battles were fought at Chawinda and Sialkot. The war ended on 23 September 1965 with a UN-sponsored ceasefire, followed by the Tashkent Declaration (January 1966). Effects: both sides returned to the pre-war positions; the Kashmir issue remained unsolved; and 6 September is celebrated as Defence Day.

lessons.title: The Afghan War, War on Terrorism and Ayub Khan's Era
lessons.notes_html:
The Afghan War

The Afghan War began in 1979 CE when the Soviet Union (USSR) sent its forces into Afghanistan. Pakistan supported the Afghan Mujahideen, with the help of the USA and other countries, until the Soviet withdrawal in 1989; civil war and then the Taliban government followed.

Impact on Pakistan

About 3-4 million Afghan refugees came to Pakistan, burdening the economy. 'Kalashnikov culture' — weapons and drugs (heroin) — spread in Pakistani society, increasing crime and addiction. After 9/11, Pakistan joined the War on Terrorism and itself faced bomb blasts and attacks in which tens of thousands of Pakistanis and soldiers were martyred; the Pakistan Army launched successful operations like Zarb-e-Azb (2014 CE) to clear the tribal areas. Pakistan's economy suffered heavy losses of over a hundred billion dollars.

The War on Terrorism

The immediate cause of the War on Terrorism was the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 (9/11) on the United States, when hijacked aeroplanes were crashed into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon. The USA blamed Al-Qaeda based in Afghanistan and launched the war; Pakistan, as a frontline ally, played an important role.

Milestones of Ayub Khan's Regime

Ayub Khan's era (1958-1969) is remembered as a decade of development: the Basic Democracies system (1959); the 1962 Constitution (presidential system); land reforms (1959); the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) and construction of Mangla and Tarbela dams; rapid industrial and agricultural development (the 'Green Revolution'); family planning; and shifting the capital to the new city of Islamabad.
